nameStory: The shortbodied cellar spider gets its name from its compact, rounded abdomen that's noticeably shorter and more globular than its long-legged cellar spider cousins. While most cellar spiders have elongated, oval bodies, this little spider looks almost like someone squeezed its body into a tight ball, making it instantly recognizable among the cellar spider family.
description: The shortbodied cellar spider is a tiny, pale spider with an unusually compact, rounded body and relatively long, thin legs. These delicate spiders are quite small, with bodies typically measuring just a few millimeters across. They're part of the cellar spider family but stand out due to their distinctive short, globular abdomen that looks almost bead-like. Originally from the Near East, they've spread around the world and occasionally turn up in New England buildings.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The abdomen is remarkably short and rounded, almost spherical, feeling firm like a tiny bead if gently touched (though best observed without handling)

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small with body length of just 2-3mm, about the size of a pinhead, making them easy to overlook

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds loose, irregular webs with no organized pattern, feeling sticky but delicate when accidentally walked through

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Has six eyes arranged in a tight cluster (unlike the eight eyes of most spiders), appearing as tiny dark dots on the pale head region

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with quick, jerky motions when disturbed, often freezing in place when a light is turned on in dark spaces

habitat: In New England, shortbodied cellar spiders are found almost exclusively in human-made structures like basements, crawl spaces, and storage areas where humidity levels stay relatively high. They prefer dark, undisturbed corners of buildings, often near foundations or in areas with poor ventilation. Since they're not native to our region, they depend on heated buildings to survive our harsh winters.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as building temperatures warm up, beginning to build new webs in forgotten corners and storage areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you're most likely to spot them moving around their webs or find egg sacs in their preferred hiding spots.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue web-building activities as they prepare for winter, often moving deeper into building interiors seeking stable temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Remain active year-round in heated buildings, though they may move less frequently and stay hidden in the warmest available spaces.

funFact: This spider is one of the few spiders in the world that has only six eyes instead of the usual eight, and it's named 'senoculata' which literally means 'six-eyed' in Latin — making it a living example of how evolution sometimes subtracts features rather than adding them!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with young long-bodied cellar spiders, but the shortbodied version looks like someone squashed a regular cellar spider's abdomen into a ball. Remember: 'short and round like a bead, long and oval feeds instead' — the long-bodied species have distinctly elongated abdomens.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'cellar spider,' this species isn't closely related to the common long-bodied cellar spiders most people know. They're both in the Pholcidae family but represent very different evolutionary branches, showing how similar lifestyles can lead to similar common names even among distant relatives.
compareHints: As the only Spermophora species recorded in New England, it's most easily compared to other cellar spiders in the Pholcidae family. Unlike the common long-bodied cellar spider (Pholcus phalangioides), the shortbodied version has a distinctly compact, rounded abdomen and only six eyes instead of eight. The body proportions are completely different — imagine comparing a marble to an olive.
